The assertion can never fail due to a torn read of display_mode even if get_display_mode() and set_display_mode_state() both lack locking, because a str reference swap is a single pointer-width store. The locking defect (F-0038) is therefore not detectable by this test on CPython.
findings.verdict_reason: On CPython, the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) makes the read and write of a single string reference atomic at the machine level. The assertion all(value in allowed for value in samples) checks that every observed value is one of the three short allowed strings. Even if the lock were removed entirely from set_display_mode_state() and get_display_mode(), any torn read of the _display_mode string reference would still yield one of the three published values (no third state exists between them), so the assertion can never fail. The locking contract F-0038 is designed to prevent observing intermediate torn state, but CPython's GIL makes that intermediate state unobservable at the test level. This test does not actually exercise the lock's protecting behavior.

findings.finder_reason: The test asserts `len(instructions) <= 5` (an upper bound only). If `disassemble()` returned an empty list — for example because the count-gating loop was accidentally changed to always return early or the `md.disasm` generator produced no output — the assertion `0 <= 5` would still pass. The production capability being tested (that `count` correctly caps decoded instructions from real PE code) could be completely non-functional (zero instructions returned) while this test stays green.
findings.verdict_reason: The production `disassemble()` method (disassembler.py lines 260-272) iterates the capstone generator and breaks when `len(instructions) >= count`. With `count=5` against `kernel32.dll`'s `.text` section (which contains thousands of valid x86-64 instructions), the function must return exactly 5 instructions. A production regression that causes the break condition to fire immediately (e.g., `>= 0` instead of `>= count`), or that causes the loop to not execute at all, or a silent empty return from `md.disasm`, would return an empty list. The assertion `assert len(instructions) <= 5` evaluates `0 <= 5` which is trivially true, so the test stays green while the count-capping feature is completely broken. No lower-bound check exists to catch this failure.
findings.recommendation: Replace `assert len(instructions) <= 5` with `assert len(instructions) == 5`. Since the input is a real `.text` section from `kernel32.dll` containing thousands of decodable x86-64 instructions, capstone must always return exactly 5 when `count=5`. This turns the check into a bidirectional gate: too many instructions (upper bound violation) and zero/fewer instructions (lower bound violation, e.g., broken loop or missing count enforcement) are both caught. If strict equality feels fragile, use `assert 1 <= len(instructions) <= 5` as a minimum, but equality is correct and stronger here.
